pages.x: Mexican gangs had long smuggled drugs into the United States, the biggest market in the world, and grew rich when cocaine routes moved through Mexico in the 1990s. Ten days after taking office in December 2006, President Felipe Calderón sent some 6,500 soldiers and federal police into his home state of Michoacán. Soon tens of thousands of troops were on the streets.

Arrests and killings of leaders split the cartels, and the pieces fought each other for the smuggling routes. The Sinaloa cartel of Joaquín Guzmán, known as El Chapo, fought the Juárez cartel for the border city of Ciudad Juárez, where more than 3,000 people were killed in 2010 alone, one of the highest murder rates in the world.

Los Zetas, a gang founded by deserters from the army's special forces, broke with the Gulf cartel in 2010 and spread terror across the northeast. In August 2010, near San Fernando in Tamaulipas, they murdered 72 migrants from Central and South America who were on their way to the United States.

In 2013 farmers and business people in Michoacán, tired of paying protection money to a cult-like cartel called the Knights Templar, took up arms themselves. Their self-defence groups drove the cartel out of many towns. The government first welcomed them, then tried to bring them under control, and some were taken over by criminals in their turn.

On the night of 26 September 2014, in Iguala, local police and gunmen attacked buses carrying students from the teachers' college of Ayotzinapa. Forty-three students were taken away and never came home. Investigators found that police and officials had worked with a local gang, and the families still ask for the whole truth.

Guzmán had escaped from prison once, in 2001. Caught in 2014, he escaped again in 2015, through a tunnel about a mile long dug to the shower of his cell. Marines recaptured him at Los Mochis in 2016. Sent to the United States, he was tried in New York and sentenced to life in prison in 2019.

President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, elected in 2018, promised "hugs, not bullets": to fight the poverty behind crime. He set up a new National Guard, made up largely of soldiers. In October 2019 soldiers caught Ovidio Guzmán, a son of El Chapo, in Culiacán, but let him go when cartel gunmen took over the city. He was caught again in 2023.

Since 2006 several hundred thousand people have been murdered in Mexico, many but not all of them in the drug war, and tens of thousands more have vanished. Mothers search the countryside for hidden graves themselves, probing the ground with iron rods, because they fear no one else will find their children.

In 2024 an old Sinaloa boss, Ismael Zambada, was flown to the United States, by force he said, and his followers and El Chapo's sons went to war. Claudia Sheinbaum, president from October 2024, promised policing led by intelligence. In 2025, pressed by the United States, Mexico sent dozens of jailed cartel figures to American courts, and her government said murders were falling.

Mexico's drug war has no clear end. Each boss caught has been replaced, and the cartels have moved into extortion, fuel theft and people smuggling. Mexicans still argue over whether soldiers on the streets made the country safer, and most guns traced from its crime scenes come from the United States.
